extracted.intended_audience: AI researchers, cognitive scientists, and computer scientists studying heuristic problem solving and Polya's methods
extracted.subtask_description: Analyse and apply Polya-style auxiliary problems and connection subproblems in mathematical/AI problem solving: how auxiliary problems are generated, how their results or methods are connected to the main problem, and what issues arise for AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary-problem method
rubrics_metrics.description: To solve problem P: 1. Find an auxiliary problem, AP. 2. Subproblem: Solve problem AP. 3. Use the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polya uses the concept broadly (including simple substitutions). The paper stresses attention to the more exotic versions that do not fit garden-variety AI transformations. The method may create several auxiliary problems and may require planning to connect them to the main problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation techniques for auxiliary problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary problems can be generated by specialization, generalization, substitutions (convertible transformations), setting up analogous lower-dimensional cases, or selecting special cases of the main problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some generated auxiliary problems are routine (e.g., symbolic substitutions) and fit existing AI operator-selection frameworks; others are 'exotic' and are weakly related to the main problem structure and thus harder for AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find result of the auxiliary problem already in the existing main problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Connection strategy: check whether the result (or a known object) from the auxiliary problem already exists as part of the main problem's figure or data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the auxiliary result is already present inside the main problem, little or no introduction/augmentation is needed; example: a triangle inside a parallelogram that matches the auxiliary triangle with known sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce result of auxiliary problem to be a component of main problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Connection strategy: augment the main problem (e.g., extend a segment, add a construction) so that the auxiliary problem's result becomes a component of the main problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This typically produces an augmented figure/problem in the same problem space as the main problem; success depends on being able to introduce the auxiliary result (e.g., extend c to create a parallelogram) and then solve the augmented problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce main problem to auxiliary problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Connection strategy: transform or reinterpret the main problem so that solving the auxiliary problem (or its solution) directly yields a solution to the main problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Two-ships example: identify a reducing transformation (difference of velocities), construct an equivalent reduced problem using operators (e.g., parallelogram of velocities), then solve that constructed problem. This often uses means-ends analysis and requires constructing the relevant problem-space operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use solution method of auxiliary problem as solution plan for main problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Connection strategy: take the method/plan used to solve the auxiliary problem and use it as a plan (schema) for the main problem, finding analog steps in the main problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using the decomposition + locus method for the triangle's center of gravity as the plan for the tetrahedron case. Requires 'plan interpreting machinery' and finding analogs for each step; mapping can be identity or an exact analog under (possibly inverse) mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful connection subproblem outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: The successful result of a connection subproblem is a well-defined intermediate problem whose solution will yield the main problem's solution and which makes essential use of the auxiliary problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This intermediate problem must be specific enough to leave the remaining details to later solving stages. It may be easy or hard (or even impossible) to solve; a flawed connection can make the overall approach fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection subproblem as a distinct class of subproblems
rubrics_metrics.description: Connection subproblems are the tasks of finding a concrete way to use an auxiliary problem's result or method in the main problem (they create relevance between problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They differ from ordinary subproblems because they manufacture a relation between problems rather than having it defined in advance. Handling them is crucial to using auxiliary problems effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tame (domesticated) vs wild auxiliary subproblems
rubrics_metrics.description: Tame subproblems: subproblems whose relation to the main problem is defined in advance by construction (typical in AI). Wild auxiliary subproblems: relations are problematical and not predefined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current AI programs can handle tame subproblems but struggle with wild ones. The diversity and unexpected relations of Polya-style auxiliary problems make many of them 'wild' and thus beyond current AI capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary problems do not form a well-defined problem space
rubrics_metrics.description: The space of auxiliary problems around a main problem lacks a clear, pre-specified structure: generators of auxiliary problems bear at best a weak relationship to the main problem's structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this, representing auxiliary problems as standard AI problem spaces (states + operators) is problematic; search strategies that assume such a space will miss many auxiliary problems or connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-ends analysis for connection subproblems
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical method for solving connection subproblems is GPS-like means-ends analysis: identify differences between main and auxiliary problems, propose reducing operators, and iteratively refine toward a constructible reduced problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Two-ships trace exemplifies this: find difference (velocity), propose applying a reducing velocity, discover constraints (must apply to everything), determine exact reducing velocity, and convert to a constructible diagram problem. Representation and operator specification are important for each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct problem spaces from givens + functional orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a connection workable, build an explicit problem space from (a) the given information of both problems and (b) the chosen high-level functional idea (e.g., reduce main problem, introduce result).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction may be feasible because much structure is present in the givens; success depends on finding appropriate operators and representations (e.g., velocity operators, geometric constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya-style heuristic components to preserve
rubrics_metrics.description: Key elements of Polya's heuristic worth preserving/using: auxiliary problems, future orientation (learning from the present problem), analogy and induction, and scattered heuristics assembled into methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI should not discard these components; rather, systems need capabilities (learning, analogy mapping, handling of wild subproblems) to exploit them fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for AI readiness to use auxiliary problems
rubrics_metrics.description: An AI system must be able to (a) generate or accept diverse auxiliary problems, (b) formulate and solve connection subproblems that tie auxiliaries to the main problem, and (c) construct/interpret plans when using auxiliary methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues current AI handles (a) and (c) only in limited contexts and largely fails at (b); progress requires explicit mechanisms for connection subproblems, richer representations, and learning/analogy capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of difficulty: connection subproblems are not proven intrinsically hard
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no indication that connection subproblems are necessarily especially difficult; they are however 'essentially unexplored' and may be tractable when attempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This serves as a research criterion: do not assume impossibility—attempt building AI systems to pose/solve connection subproblems to test tractability.
